rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening may be a new independent sentence or connected to what precedes; al-Ālūsī favors the soundest Arabic reading with least strain.
rows.anchor: جملة مستأنفة وابتداء كلام أو متعلقة بما قبلها

rows.speaker: الواحدي
rows.claim: Al-Wāḥidī takes “that” as the Book promised to Muḥammad in 73:5.
rows.anchor: ذلك إشارة إلى الكتاب الموعود به صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم بقوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another proposed referent is the Book promised through Moses and Jesus, with the earlier community’s expectation in 2:89 offered as support.
rows.anchor: أو على لسان موسى وعيسى عليهما السلام لقوله تعالى : ( وكانوا من قبل يستفتحون

rows.speaker: كعب
rows.claim: Kaʿb urges adherence to the Qur’an as intellect’s understanding, wisdom’s light, and knowledge’s springs.
rows.anchor: ما روي عن كعب عليكم بالقرآن فإنه فهم العقل ونور الحكمة وينابيع العلم

rows.speaker: كعب
rows.claim: The same report calls the Qur’an the newest book in covenant with God and quotes the Torah’s promise of a new revelation to Muḥammad that opens blind eyes, deaf ears, and closed hearts.
rows.anchor: وقال في التوراة يامحمد إني منزل عليك توراة حديثة تفتح بها أعينا عميا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The demonstrative may point to the Qur’an before its audience, with distance expressing exalted rank; al-Sakkākī’s explanation is preferred.
rows.anchor: والإشارة بذلك للتعظيم وتنزيل البعد الرتبي منزلة البعد الحقيقي كما في قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A possible explanation is that revelation became “that” once it descended from the divine presence and was conveyed to people, as something separated from its source.
rows.anchor: أو لأنه لما نزل عن حضرة الربوبية وصار بحضرتنا بعد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A poet’s maxim that whatever is not in one’s hand is distant supports the separation-based explanation.
rows.anchor: كل ما ليس في يديك بعيد

rows.speaker: السهيلي
rows.claim: Al-Suhaylī explains the contrast with 6:92’s “this Book” by the different settings, including the opening disjointed letters in this sūra.
rows.anchor: حروف التهجي في الأول وهي تقطع بها الحروف وهو لا يكون إلا في حقنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A far-fetched explanation treats the Qur’an as a transient utterance: each part vanishes as it is produced and so is distant from the senses.
rows.anchor: القرآن لفظ وهو من قبيل الأعراض السيالة الغير القارة

rows.speaker: الجرجاني
rows.claim: Al-Jurjānī transmits a group’s view that near and far demonstratives can alternate, citing Qur’anic examples from the story of Jesus.
rows.anchor: ونقله الجرجاني عن طائفة وأنشدوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cited verse may use “that” for someone famous or previously spoken of, so the poem does not prove that a far form simply means “this.”
rows.anchor: أقول له والرمح يأطر متنه تأمل خفافا إنني أنا ذلكا

rows.speaker: الإمام الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī’s claim that “that” is distant by convention but not by linguistic form conflicts with what Arabic grammar authorities teach.
rows.anchor: وقول الإمام الرازي إن ذلك للبعيد عرفا لا وضعا فحمله هنا

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: Al-ʿIkrima’s identification with the Torah and Gospel is acceptable only if supported by an authentic report; otherwise al-Ālūsī rejects it.
rows.anchor: والقول بأن الإشارة إلى التوراة والإنجيل كما نقل عن عكرمة إن كان قد ورد فيه حديث صحيح قبلناه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A highly unusual view makes “that” the straight path requested in al-Fātiḥa and thereby links al-Baqara to it; al-Ālūsī calls this far-fetched.
rows.anchor: وأغرب ما رأيناه في توجيه الإشارة أنها إلى الصراط المستقيم في الفاتحة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī’s preferred referent is the Qur’an, with rank-distance as in al-Sakkākī’s account and the radiance of nearness still apparent.
rows.anchor: والذي تنفتح له الآذان أنه إشارة إلى القرآن ووجه البعد ما ذكره صاحب المفتاح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Demonstratives normally indicate sensory objects; for the imperceptible or an unseen perceptible thing, they make it present as though witnessed.
rows.anchor: والمعتبر في أسماء الإشارة هو الإشارة الحسية التي لا يتصور تعلقها إلا بمحسوس مشاهد

rows.speaker: الرضي
rows.claim: Al-Raḍī describes this treatment of unseen referents as making rational indication stand in place of sensory indication.
rows.anchor: وتنزيل الإشارة العقلية منزلة الحسية كما في الرضى

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī rejects the claim that a demonstrative need not refer to something perceptible whenever it has an adjectival modifier.
rows.anchor: وقول بعضهم أن اسم الإشارة إذا كان معه صفة له لم يلزم أن يكون محسوسا وهم

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Al-Rāghib traces “book” to joining one piece of leather to another by sewing; ordinary writing joins letters.
rows.anchor: قال الراغب ضم أديم إلى أديم بالخياطة وفي المتعارف ضم الحروف بعضها إلى بعض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Writing originally orders letters in script; “book” can also name anything conjoined in speech, and the terms are metaphorically exchanged.
rows.anchor: والأصل في الكتابة النظم بالخط وقد يقال ذلك للمضموم وبعضه إلى بعض باللفظ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an is called God’s Book even though it is not a physical written book, since “book” extends to composed revelation.
rows.anchor: ولذا سمى كتاب الله وإن لم يكن كتابا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Book” can remain a verbal noun used for its object emphatically, or mean the object itself; it names the Qur’an’s composed utterance before script records it.
rows.anchor: والكتاب هنا إما باق على المصدرية وسمى به المفعول للمبالغة أو هو بمعنى المفعول

rows.speaker: الإمام
rows.claim: The proposed derivations from collecting things, gathering troops, repelling doubts, containing all knowledge, or assembling duties are a fabricated explanation.
rows.anchor: وقول الإمامإن اشتقاق الكتاب من كتبت الشيء إذا جمعته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The article in “the Book” is generic and marks the Qur’an as the perfect book deserving the name above other heavenly books.
rows.anchor: واللام في الكتاب للحقيقة مثلها في أنت الرجل

rows.speaker: ابن عصفور
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṣfūr says the article after a demonstrative, in a vocative with ayy, and after sudden idhā is presentational and referential.
rows.anchor: كل لام وقعت بعد اسم الإشارة وأي في النداء وإذا الفجائية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A variant reading is reported as “tanẓīl al-kitāb.”
rows.anchor: وقريء تنزيل الكتاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rayb originally names the unease a thing causes, then extends to troubling events and inner stirrings such as anger.
rows.anchor: والريب الشك وأصله مصدر رابني الشيء إذا حصل فيك الريبة وهي قلق النفس

rows.speaker: الإمام الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī explains temporal calamities and inner agitation as forms of doubt because they are uncertain; al-Ālūsī rejects this derivation.
rows.anchor: وقول الإمام الرازي : إن هذين قد يرجعان إلى معنى الشك

rows.speaker: أبو زيد
rows.claim: Abū Zayd distinguishes rābanī, when one is certain of a troubling matter, from arābanī, when one suspects it without certainty.
rows.anchor: وفرق أبو زيد بين رابني وأرابني فيقال رابني من فلان أمر إذا كنت مستيقنا

rows.speaker: بشار
rows.claim: Bashshār’s verse witnesses the distinction: a friend says “I only suspected” when the matter is doubted, but speaks directly when certain.
rows.anchor: أخوك الذي إن ربته قال إنما أراب وإن عاتبته لان جانبه

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some lexicographers distinguish rayb from ordinary doubt by adding an element of accusation or suspicion.
rows.anchor: وبعض فرق بين الريب والشك بأن الريب شك مع تهمة

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Al-Rāghib defines doubt as equal hesitation between two alternatives without a preponderating sign.
rows.anchor: وقال الراغب : الشك وقوف النفس بين شيئين متقابلين

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Al-Rāghib derives mirya from rubbing an udder to draw milk and uses it for hesitation that seeks an indication.
rows.anchor: والمرية التردد في المتقابلين وطلب الأمارة من مري الضرع

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: For al-Rāghib, rayb is imagining something about an object, then finding that the suspicion was mistaken.
rows.anchor: والريب أن يتوهم في الشيء ثم ينكشف عما توهم فيه

rows.speaker: الجولي
rows.claim: Al-Jūlī distinguishes doubt, which may fall short of decisive clarity, from rayb, which has some appearance but not certainty.
rows.anchor: وقال الجولي : يقال الشك لما استوى فيه الاعتقاد أن أو لم يستويا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrasing is apt because rayb falls short of certainty while showing itself somewhat; negating rayb therefore rules out even lesser uncertainty.
rows.anchor: حسن هنا ( لا ريب فيه ) للإشارة إلى أنه لا يحصل فيه ريب فضلا عن شك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Despite many who doubt it, the Qur’an’s elevated rank and manifest proof leave no rational person in doubt after reflection that it is revelation from God.
rows.anchor: ونفى سبحانه الريب فيه مع كثرة المرتابين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation supplies an omitted “cause”: the Qur’an contains none of the obscurity, complexity, contradiction, or unsupported claims that cause doubt.
rows.anchor: وقيل إنه على الحذف كأنه قال لا سبب ريب فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another reading takes the declarative form as a prohibition: “Do not doubt it,” by analogy with the prohibition in 2:197.
rows.anchor: وقيل معناه النهي وإن كان لفظه خبرا أي لا ترتابوا فيه على حد ( لا رفث ولا فسوق )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A syntactic option makes “in it” an adjective of “doubt” and “for the godfearing” the predicate: no doubt in it for them.
rows.anchor: للمتقين فالظرف صفة وللمتقين خبر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On another parse, “guidance” is a circumstantial accusative from the pronoun in “in it,” describing the Book as guiding while free of doubt.
rows.anchor: حال من الضمير المجرور أي لا ريب كائنا فيه للمتقين حال كونه هاديا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the author’s parse, lā negates the noun’s predicate quality, not a restricted subset of the noun, preserving comprehensive negation.
rows.anchor: لنفي اتصاف الاسم بالخبر لا لنفي قيد الاسم فلا تتوجه إليه

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says fronting “in it” avoids suggesting that this Book lacks a defect found in other books, unlike 37:47’s contrast with worldly wine.
rows.anchor: وإنما لم يقل سبحانه لا فيه ريب على حد ( لا فيها غول )

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān denies that fronting the predicate here conveys exclusivity; al-Ālūsī dismisses that objection.
rows.anchor: حتى أنكر أبو حيان إفادة تقديم الخبر هنا الحصر وهو مما لا يلتفت إليه

rows.speaker: سليم أبو الشعثاء
rows.claim: Sulaym Abū al-Shaʿthāʾ reads raybun in the nominative; negating one instance differs from the common reading’s comprehensive negation.
rows.anchor: وقرأ سليم أبو الشعثاء لا ريب فيه بالرفع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the common reading, lā negates all instances of doubt rather than merely denying that doubt is universal.
rows.anchor: فلا لعموم النفي لا لنفي العموم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most readers pause after “in it,” making the Book itself the guidance, a usage repeated elsewhere in the Qur’an.
rows.anchor: والوقف على ( فيه ) هو المشهور وعليه يكون الكتاب نفسه هدى

rows.speaker: نافع وعاصم
rows.claim: Nāfiʿ and ʿĀṣim pause after “no doubt,” treating the predicate as omitted.
rows.anchor: وعن نافع وعاصم الوقف على ( لا ريب ) ولا ريب في حذف الخبر

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj interprets lā rayb as “truly” and treats the pause after it as complete, though al-Ālūsī ranks this below the common pause.
rows.anchor: وذهب الزجاج إلى جعل ( لا ريب ) بمعنى حقا فالوقف عليه تام

rows.speaker: ابن كثير
rows.claim: Ibn Kathīr links the pronominal hāʾ to a preceding silent yāʾ; when preceded by another silent consonant it is linked with wāw.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن كثير فيهي بوصل الهاء ياء في اللفظ

rows.speaker: حفص
rows.claim: Ḥafṣ agrees with the linked hāʾ in “fīhi muhānan,” “mulāqīhi,” and “sa-uṣlīhi.”
rows.anchor: ووافقه حفص في ( فيه مهانا ) وملاقيه وسأصليه

rows.speaker: الزهري وابن جندب
rows.claim: Al-Zuhrī and Ibn Jundub read pronominal hāʾs with ḍamma throughout the Qur’an, following the original form.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الزهري وابن جندب بضم الهاء من الكنايات في جميع القرآن

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Hudā is originally a verbal noun or a substitute for one; Sibawayh counts fuʿal as a rare verbal-noun pattern.
rows.anchor: والهدى ( في الأصل مصدر هدى أو عوض عن المصدر وكل في كلام سيبويه

rows.speaker: الشاطبي
rows.claim: Al-Shāṭibī cites poetry to illustrate the rare verbal-noun pattern with the word liqā.
rows.anchor: الشاطبي وأنشد : وقد زعموا حلما لقاك فلم أزد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here hudā functions as an active participle through a familiar nominal usage.
rows.anchor: والمراد منه هنا اسم الفاعل بأحد الوجوه المعروفة في أمثاله

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya treats hudā as feminine in gender.
rows.anchor: وهو لفظ مؤنث عند ابن عطية ومذكر عند اللحياني

rows.speaker: اللحياني والفراء
rows.claim: Al-Liḥyānī treats hudā as masculine, while Banū Asad use it as feminine according to al-Farrāʾ.
rows.anchor: ومذكر عند اللحياني وبنو أسد يؤنثون كما قال الفراء

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī defines guidance as direction that actually brings its recipient to the desired goal.
rows.anchor: وفي الكشاف هي الدلالة الموصلة إلى البغية

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī argues that guidance reaches the goal because it is opposed to misguidance, which is failure to reach it.
rows.anchor: واستدل عليه بثلاثة وجوه الأول وقوع الضلال في مقابله

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: He also argues that “guided” is praise like “rightly guided”; mere instruction without attaining the path does not earn that description.
rows.anchor: والثاني أنه يقال مهدي في موضع المدح كمهتد

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: His third argument is that ihtadā is the mutāwaʿ form of hadā, supposedly carrying the base verb’s meaning as “broke” carries into “became broken.”
rows.anchor: والثالث أن اهتدى مطاوع هدى ولن يكون المطاوع في خلاف معنى أصله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī objects that the first contrast concerns intransitive guidance or being guided; transitive guidance is opposed by leading astray, so the contrast proves no lexical arrival.
rows.anchor: أما أولا فلأن المذكور في مقابلة الضلالة هو الهدى اللازم بمعنى الاهتداء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even if misguidance means failure to reach, that is only a possible consequence; it does not establish arrival as part of the meaning of guidance.
rows.anchor: بل هو العدول عن الطريق الموصل إلى البغية فيكون الهدى عبارة عن الدلالة على الطريق الموصل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fact that “guided” is usually said only of one who has attained the goal can reflect common usage, not the lexical meaning of guidance itself.
rows.anchor: وأما ثانيا فلأنا لا نسلم أن الضلالة عبارة عن الخيبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb ihtadā need not be a true mutāwaʿ of hadā; it can describe the recipient’s separate action of following the path after being shown it.
rows.anchor: وأما رابعا فلأنا لا نسلم أن اهتدى مطاوع هدى بل هو من قبيل أمره فأتمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase hadāhu fa-ihtadā means that he showed him the road and the recipient then travelled it; “He guided him but he did not follow” is possible.
rows.anchor: بدليل أنه يقال هداه فلم يهتد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The existence of an action does not always entail its mutāwaʿ; in the Mukhtār agreement is unnecessary, while other verb classes require it.
rows.anchor: قالوا : لا يلزم من وجود الفعل وجود مطاوعه مطلقا ففي المختار لا يجب أن يوافق المطاوع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an says God sends signs for warning but that warning may increase people’s defiance rather than produce fear, showing that an action’s effect may fail.
rows.anchor: مع قوله سبحانه ( ونخوفهم فما يزيدهم إلا طغيانا )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The difference between mutāwaʿ verbs that must or need not match their base verb is treated at length in ʿUrūs al-afrāḥ.
rows.anchor: والفرق بينهما مفصل في عروس الأفراح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qur’anic uses of guidance without arrival at the goal challenge al-Zamakhsharī’s definition of guidance as necessarily reaching the goal.
rows.anchor: ليس فيه وصول إلى البغية وقد مر بعضه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Scholars variously hold that guidance literally means general direction and figuratively means successful direction, the reverse, both by homonymy, or a shared common sense.
rows.anchor: ولهذا اختلفوا هل هي حقيقة في الدلالة المطلقة مجاز في غيرها أو بالعكس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage records competing attributions of the two definitions to Ashʿarites and Muʿtazilites, while noting that the popular attribution reverses them.
rows.anchor: والمذكور في كلام الأشاعرة أن المختار عندهم ما ذكر في الكشاف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The proposed reconciliation assigns the Ashʿarite definition to technical religious usage and the popular definition to ordinary language, but al-Ālūsī argues it should be reversed.
rows.anchor: والتوفيق بأن كلام الأشاعرة في المعنى الشرعي والمشهور مبني على المعنى اللغوي أو العرفي يخدشه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī’s final position is that guidance covers both meanings and preventing destruction, resolving much of the dispute.
rows.anchor: والحق عند أهل الحق أن الهداية مشتركة بين المعنيين المذكورين وعدم الإهلاك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muttaqīn is the plural active participle of ittaqā; its root begins with wāw, and the tāʾ belongs to the derived form.
rows.anchor: والمتقين ( جمع متق اسم فاعل من وقاه فأتقى فقاؤه واو لا تاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wiqāya means protection generally; in religious usage taqwā is protecting oneself from what harms in the afterlife.
rows.anchor: والوقاية لغة الصيانة مطلقا وشرعا صيانة المرء نفسه عما يضر في الآخرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first level of taqwā is avoiding association with God.
rows.anchor: فأولاها التوقي عن الشرك والثانية عن الكبائر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second level is avoiding major sins, including persistence in minor sins.
rows.anchor: عن الكبائرومنها الإصرار على الصغائر

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: A report transmitted by al-Tirmidhī from the Prophet says a servant does not reach taqwā until leaving harmless things out of caution against harmful ones; al-Ālūsī gives no grading.
rows.anchor: ما رواه الترمذي عنه صلى الله عليه وسلم لا يبلغ العبد أن يكون من المتقين حتى يدع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The third level therefore includes avoiding minor sins as well as the doubtful, out of caution.
rows.anchor: وفي هذه المرتبة يعتبر ترك الصغائر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A poem defines the wary person as one who leaves both major and minor sins, careful even of small dangers.
rows.anchor: خل الذنوب كبيرها وصغيرها فهو التقي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One definition of taqwā is that God does not find a person where He forbade him and does not miss him where He commanded him.
rows.anchor: التقوى أن لا يراك الله حيث نهاك ولا يفقدك حيث أمرك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other definitions are disavowing one’s own power and avoiding anything that distracts the heart’s innermost self from God.
rows.anchor: التبري عن الحول والقوة وقيل : التنزه عن كل ما يشغل السر عن الحق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A Sufi poet says that even a momentary thought of desiring anything besides God would make him judge himself an apostate.
rows.anchor: ولو خطرت لي في سواك إرادة على خاطري سهوا حكمت بردتي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Book’s guidance encompasses people at all levels of taqwā.
rows.anchor: وهداية الكتاب المبين شاملة لأرباب هذه المراتب أجمعين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If guidance means bringing people to the first level, “the godfearing” can mean those approaching it, a prospective metaphor used concisely to honor God’s allies.
rows.anchor: فإن أريد بكونه ( هدى للمتقين ) إرشاده إياهم إلى تحصيل المرتبة الأولى فالمراد بهم المشارفون مجازا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prospective reading suits the sūra’s opening praise of God’s allies; the following description of believers can refer to the time the guidance relation is established.
rows.anchor: وإيثاره على العبارة المعربة عن ذلك للإيجاز وتصدير السورة الكريمة بذكر أوليائه تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reading the whole phrase as a direct answer to “who are the godfearing?” and making all its referents prospective is rejected as contrary to the flow.
rows.anchor: وحمل الكل على المشارفة يأباه السوق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the Book guides one rank upward, the expression is literal when the godfearing are at the lower rank and figurative when they already occupy the target rank.
rows.anchor: فإن عني بالمتقين أصحاب المرتبة الأولى تعينت الحقيقة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Likewise, if guidance is toward the third level, calling people at the second level godfearing is literal; calling those already at the third level so makes guidance figurative.
rows.anchor: فإن أريد بالهدى الإرشاد إلى تحصيل المرتبة الثالثة فإن عني بالمتقين أصحاب المرتبة الثانية تعينت الحقيقة

rows.speaker: مولانا مفتي الديار الرومية
rows.claim: When guidance would advance people already at the highest rank, the guidance is figurative while “godfearing” remains literal, according to the Ottoman mufti.
rows.anchor: كذا حققه مولانا مفتي الديار الرومية ومنه يعلم اندفاع

rows.speaker: مولانا مفتي الديار الرومية
rows.claim: The mufti answers the objection that guidance for the already guided is tautological, whether guidance is defined as arrival or direction.
rows.anchor: ومنه يعلم اندفاع ما قيل أن الهداية إن فسرت بالدلالة الموصلة يقتضي أن يكون

rows.speaker: بعض المحققين
rows.claim: Another investigator says no metaphor is needed: as a weapon is protection for the protected and wealth is richness for the rich, the Book truly guides those already guided.
rows.anchor: إذا قيل السلاح عصمة للمعتصم والمال غنى للغني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For derived predicates, the relevant time is when the relation is asserted, according to the established view of the precise scholars.
rows.anchor: والذي عليه المحققون أنه زمان النسبة

rows.speaker: السبكي والكرماني
rows.claim: Al-Subkī and al-Kirmānī hold that “whoever kills a man gets his spoils” is literal, rejecting the claim that the derived predicate is figurative.
rows.anchor: وقد ذهب السبكي والكرماني إلى أن من قتل قتيلا فله سلبه حقيقة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The killer example is meaningful because a contextual cue makes the claim exclusive: the killing was done by this person rather than another.
rows.anchor: فكأنه قيل لم يشاركه فيه غيره فسلبه له دون غيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With a demonstrative such as “I squeezed this wine,” the relevant time for whether the description is literal is the time of pointing, not the earlier judgment.
rows.anchor: والمعتبر زمان الإشارة لا زمان الحكم السابق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an remains guidance despite containing ambiguous and difficult passages, since guidance need not be supplied by every individual part.
rows.anchor: ثم لا يقدح في كونه هدى ما فيه من المجمل والمتشابه لأنه لا يستلزم كونه هدى هدايته باعتبار كل جزء منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the ambiguous material does not lack an explanation of its intent; on the Shāfiʿī view it guides once clarified.
rows.anchor: أو لأن ذلك لا ينفك عن بيان المراد منه كما ذهب إليه الشافعية

rows.speaker: الإمام
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī argues that the Qur’an cannot guide to truths on which its own authority depends, such as God’s existence and attributes and proof of prophecy, lest circularity follow.
rows.anchor: فقد نص الإمام على أنه كل ما يتوقف صحة كون القرآن حجة على صحته لا يكون القرآن هدى فيه

rows.speaker: بعض المحققين
rows.claim: Some scholars hold that reflection on the Qur’an’s rational proofs can guide even to knowledge of God; 2:185 is cited in support.
rows.anchor: وبعض صحح أن القرآن في نفسه هدى في كل شيء حتى معرفة الله تعالى لمن تأمل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mentioning only the godfearing praises those who benefit from the Qur’an’s guidance, just as 79:45 singles out those who fear the Hour though the Prophet warns everyone.
rows.anchor: ويكون الاقتصار على المتقين هنا بناء على تفسيرنا الهداية مدحا لهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who do not believe remain outside its benefit: 17:45 describes a veiled barrier and 17:82 says it increases wrongdoers only in loss.
rows.anchor: وإذا قرأت القرآن جعلنا بينك وبين الذين لا يؤمنون بالآخرة حجابا مستورا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī rejects supplying an omitted “and disbelievers” after “godfearing,” by analogy with the verse about garments protecting from heat.
rows.anchor: هدى للمتقين والكافرين فحذف لدلالة المتقين على حد ( سرابيل تقيكم الحر )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening’s clauses cohere: the disjointed letters gesture, “that Book” confirms its uniqueness, “no doubt” confirms one pillar, and guidance confirms the other.
rows.anchor: ( الم ) أشارت إلى ما أشارت و ( ذلك الكتاب ) قررت بعض إشارتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One rhetorical reconstruction answers why the Qur’an is miraculous: it is fully excellent in wording and meaning, which makes it the complete Book.
rows.anchor: وقيل : بالحمل على الاستئناف كأنه سئل ما باله صار معجزا فأجيب بأنه كامل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In that reconstruction, “no doubt” answers why this alone deserves the title of complete Book, and “guidance” supplies proof through its religious and worldly benefits.
rows.anchor: ثم سئل عن مقتضى الاختصاص بكونه هو الكتاب الكامل فأجيب بأنه لا يحوم حوله ريب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an’s inimitability entails its perfection; eloquent perfection removes doubt about its truth, which in turn makes it guidance.
rows.anchor: وقد يقال الإعجاز مستلزم غاية الكمال وغاية كمال الكلام البليغ ببعده من الريب والشبه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the clauses’ meanings converge, the second confirms the first; if the first entails the next, it functions like a badal of inclusion, and omission of conjunction signals their tight bond.
rows.anchor: فإن نظر إلى اتحاد المعاني بحسب المآل كان الثاني مقررا للأول فلذا ترك العطف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After classifying believers, disbelievers, and hypocrites and describing their outcomes, the discourse turns to address all people directly.
rows.anchor: لما بين سبحانه فرق المكلفين وقسمهم إلى مؤمنين وكفار ومذبذبين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preceding descriptions include the believers’ guidance and success, the disbelievers’ sealed hearts and great punishment, and the hypocrites’ diseased hearts and painful punishment.
rows.anchor: وفي الثانية ( سواء عليهم ) وفي الثالثة ( يخادعون الله ) وشرح ما ترجع إليه أحوالهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The shift to direct address is an iltifāt that rouses people to listen and directs their hearts toward receiving the message.
rows.anchor: أقبل عز شأنه عليهم بالخطاب على نهج الالتفات هزا لهم إلى الإصغاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sweet intimacy of direct address eases the burden involved in worship; the rhetorical effect need only occur for some of the audience.
rows.anchor: وجبرا لما في العبادة من الكلفة بلذيذ المخاطبة ويكفي للنكتة الوجود في البعض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The correct view is that yā is a vocative particle, not a noun or a verb, and it was originally used to call someone distant.
rows.anchor: حرف لا اسم فعل على الصحيح وضع لنداء البعيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other grammarians take yā for any vocative or say it is shared by the classes of vocative.
rows.anchor: لمطلق النداء أو مشتركة بين أقسامه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A near addressee may be called “distant” because of the caller’s or addressee’s rank, the listener’s inattention, or to stress urgency and encourage compliance.
rows.anchor: وعلى الأول ينادي بها القريب لتنزيله منزلة غيره إما لعلو مرتبة المنادي أو المنادي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The distance-based urgency may be analyzed as metonymy or as a dependent or implicit metaphor with its imagined image.
rows.anchor: فأستعمل في لازم معناه على أنه مجاز مرسل أو استعارة تبعية في الحرف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yā with its vocative noun, overt or understood, forms a complete performative utterance, equivalent to an invocation.
rows.anchor: وهو مع المنادي المنصوب لفظا أو تقديرا به لنيابته عن نحو ناديت الإنشائي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In a vocative, ayy is an indefinite meaning “some of all”; the vocative makes it definite and lets it introduce a noun with the article.
rows.anchor: والواقعة في النداء نكرة موضوعة لبعض من كل ثم تعرفت بالنداء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yā normally cannot directly precede an al-defined noun other than God, since two definiteness markers like two identical letters do not combine except rarely.
rows.anchor: لا يدخل عليها في غير الله إلا شذوذا لتعذر الجمع بين حرفي التعريف

rows.speaker: المازني
rows.claim: Al-Māzinī permits accusative ayy, but al-Ālūsī rejects this as unsupported by transmitted usage.
rows.anchor: خلافا للمازني فإنه أجاز نصبه وليس له في ذلك سلف ولا خلف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ayy takes the vocative’s ḍamma even though its following description is normally subordinate, because the description becomes the intended object of address.
rows.anchor: وأعطيت حكم المنادي وجعل المقصود بالنداء وصفا لها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Unlike ordinary adjectives, this vocative description need not be morphologically derived; it clarifies an ambiguous referent.
rows.anchor: ومن هنا لم يشترطوا في هذا الوصف الاشتقاق مع أن النحويين إلا النذر كابن الحاجب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The required hāʾ of attention adds emphasis and compensates for an expected genitive complement or tanwīn, as in the expression ayyāman tadʿū.
rows.anchor: التنبيهية زائدة لازمة للتأكيد والتعويض عما تستحق من المضاف إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an often uses this vocative pattern for repeated emphasis, clarification after ambiguity, the attention particle, and two markers of definiteness.
rows.anchor: وكثر النداء في الكتاب المجيد على هذه الطريقة لما فيها من التأكيد

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash instead analyzes ayy as a relative pronoun whose clause opening is obligatorily omitted; he cites its frequent relative and rare adjectival uses.
rows.anchor: وقطع الأخفش لضعف نظره بأن ( أيا ) الواقعة في النداء موصولة حذف صدر صلتها وجوبا

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: On al-Akhfash’s analysis, yā attaches to a form already built on ḍamma and does not alter it.
rows.anchor: فحرف النداء على هذا يكون داخلا على مبني على الضم ولم يغيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī prefers the majority analysis because it needs no deletion, fits ayy as an adjective, and avoids restrictions on what may follow a relative pronoun.
rows.anchor: ويؤيد الأول عدم الاحتياج إلى الحذف وصدق تعريف النعت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī notes that some earlier Arab grammarians found a difficult objection to the majority analysis, but this excerpt does not state the objection.
rows.anchor: نعم أورد عليه إشكال أستصعبه بعض من سلف من علماء العربية
